q: A 58-year-old patient with acute inferior wall myocardial infarction develops a heart rate of 38 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg, and dizziness. What is the FIRST-LINE emergency drug of choice?
e: Symptomatic bradycardia (HR <50 with hypotension/altered mentation) is treated first with IV Atropine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes (max 3 mg) per AHA ACLS guidelines.

q: Which laboratory finding is the MOST specific and sensitive biomarker for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction (AMI)?
e: High-sensitivity cardiac Troponin I and T are the gold-standard biomarkers for myocardial necrosis, rising within 2–4 hours and remaining elevated for 7–14 days.

q: A patient with liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension presents with hematemesis from esophageal varices. Which vasoactive medication is commonly infused to reduce portal venous pressure?
e: Octreotide (a somatostatin analogue) causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, reducing portal venous inflow and variceal bleeding pressure alongside endoscopic band ligation.

q: In a patient with acute pancreatitis, bluish discoloration observed around the umbilicus indicates retroperitoneal hemorrhage and is known as:
e: Cullen's sign is periumbilical ecchymosis; Grey Turner's sign is flank ecchymosis. Both indicate severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis or retroperitoneal bleeding.

q: A patient with acute ischemic stroke arrives at the emergency department 90 minutes after symptom onset. After ruling out intracranial hemorrhage on non-contrast CT, what is the maximum standard therapeutic window for IV Alteplase (rt-PA)?
o: Within 4.5 hours of last known well
e: Standard IV thrombolysis with Alteplase/Tenecteplase is indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset (last known normal) once hemorrhage and contraindications are excluded.

q: According to AHA 2020/2025 Adult Basic Life Support (BLS) guidelines, what is the recommended chest compression depth and rate during high-quality CPR?
e: High-quality adult CPR requires compression depth of 5–6 cm (at least 2 inches, not exceeding 2.4 inches) at a rate of 100–120/min with full chest recoil and minimal interruptions.

q: Which temperature, pressure, and holding time represent the standard hospital steam autoclaving cycle for surgical instruments?
e: Moist heat sterilization (autoclaving) at 121°C (250°F) under 15 psi for 15–20 minutes destroys all vegetative bacteria, viruses, fungi, and bacterial spores.

q: What is the standard insertion angle for an intradermal (ID) injection such as the Mantoux tuberculin skin test?
e: Intradermal injections are administered at a 10–15 degree angle with the bevel up into the epidermis/dermis to raise a distinct 6–10 mm wheal/bleb.

q: In Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL), what is the WHO-recommended first-line uterotonic dose administered immediately after delivery of the baby?
e: AMTSL consists of Oxytocin 10 IU IM (drug of choice within 1 minute of birth), controlled cord traction (Brandt-Andrews maneuver), and uterine tone assessment.

q: Under the Pritchard regimen for eclampsia, what is the standard total loading dose of Magnesium Sulfate (MgSO4)?
o: 4 g IV over 3–5 min + 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock) = 14 g total
e: The Pritchard loading regimen delivers 14 g MgSO4 total: 4 g (20% solution) slowly IV over 3–5 minutes plus 10 g (50% solution, 5 g deep IM in each buttock), followed by 5 g IM every 4 hours.

q: In the modified WHO Partograph, plotting of cervical dilation begins when the laboring woman enters active labor at what minimum cervical dilation?
o: 4 cm (or 5 cm per WHO Labour Care Guide)
e: On the classic modified WHO Partograph, the alert line starts at 4 cm cervical dilation (expected progress >=1 cm/hour); the newer WHO Labour Care Guide defines active first stage starting at 5 cm.

q: At what age does a healthy infant normally double and triple their birth weight?
o: Doubles by 3 months; triples by 9 months
Doubles by 5–6 months; triples by 12 months
Doubles by 9 months; triples by 24 months
Doubles by 12 months; triples by 36 months
e: Normal infant weight gain: doubles birth weight by 5–6 months, triples by 1 year (12 months), and quadruples by 2 years.

q: Under India's National Immunization Schedule (NIS), which oral vaccines are administered at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age?
e: At 6, 10, and 14 weeks under NIS, infants receive oral OPV-1/2/3 and oral Rotavirus vaccine (RVV-1/2/3), along with injectable Pentavalent, fIPV (6 & 14 wks), and PCV (6 & 14 wks).

q: In Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP), what is the target pre-ductal SpO2 and compression-to-ventilation ratio if heart rate remains <60 bpm despite 30 seconds of effective positive pressure ventilation (PPV)?
e: Neonatal resuscitation uses a 3:1 compression-to-ventilation ratio (120 events/min: 90 compressions + 30 ventilations) using the two-thumb encircling hands technique because newborn arrest is primarily respiratory.

q: In epidemiological screening tests, the ability of a test to correctly identify individuals who truly HAVE the disease is called:
e: Sensitivity = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives) — measures how well a test detects true disease (SnNout: high sensitivity rules out disease when negative).

q: Under the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP), what is the standard daily FDC treatment duration for newly diagnosed drug-sensitive pulmonary TB?
o: 6 months (2 months HRZE intensive + 4 months HRE continuation)
e: NTEP daily regimen for drug-sensitive TB is 6 months total: 2 months Intensive Phase (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) + 4 months Continuation Phase (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Ethambutol).

q: A patient with schizophrenia repeats the exact words spoken by the nurse immediately after hearing them. This speech disturbance is termed:
e: Echolalia is pathological repetition of another person's spoken words; echopraxia is imitating another person's movements; neologism is coining newly invented words.

q: What is the therapeutic serum lithium level range for maintenance therapy in bipolar disorder?
e: Therapeutic maintenance serum lithium is 0.6–1.2 mEq/L (acute mania 0.8–1.2 mEq/L). Toxicity starts above 1.5 mEq/L and becomes life-threatening >2.0 mEq/L.

q: Which specific antidote is administered to reverse acute acetaminophen (paracetamol) hepatotoxicity?
e: N-Acetylcysteine replenishes hepatic glutathione stores to detoxify NAPQI, the hepatotoxic metabolite of paracetamol; it is most effective when started within 8 hours of overdose.

q: Which heart valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle?
e: The mitral (bicuspid) valve guards the left atrioventricular orifice; the tricuspid valve separates the right atrium and right ventricle.

q: A patient with traumatic head injury opens eyes to pain (2), utters incomprehensible sounds (2), and shows abnormal flexion/decorticate posturing to pain (3). What is the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
e: GCS = Eye (2) + Verbal (2) + Motor (3) = 7. A GCS score <=8 indicates severe head injury/coma and typically requires definitive airway protection (intubation).

q: Cushing's triad is a late ominous clinical sign of severely increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and brain herniation. Which set of vitals represents Cushing's triad?
o: Widening pulse pressure (systolic hypertension), bradycardia, and irregular respirations
e: Cushing's triad = systolic hypertension with widening pulse pressure + reflex bradycardia + irregular respirations (Cheyne-Stokes/Biot's) due to brainstem compression.

q: Which early ECG change is classically seen in acute hyperkalemia (serum K+ >6.0 mEq/L)?
o: Prominent U waves and flattened T waves
Delta waves with short PR interval
e: Hyperkalemia produces tall peaked T waves first, followed by prolonged PR interval, flattened/absent P waves, widened QRS, and sine-wave ventricular fibrillation. Hypokalemia causes prominent U waves.

q: In emergency management of severe hyperkalemia (K+ 7.2 mEq/L) with ECG changes, which drug is given FIRST to immediately stabilize the myocardial cell membrane?
o: IV Calcium gluconate 10% (10 mL over 2–5 min)
e: IV 10% Calcium gluconate acts within 1–3 minutes to antagonize cardiac membrane excitability and prevent fatal arrhythmias (it does not lower serum K+, so IV Regular Insulin + Dextrose follows to shift K+ intracellularly).

q: Which diagnostic maneuver elicits carpal spasm (flexion of wrist and thumb adduction) within 3 minutes of inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure in hypocalcemia?
e: Trousseau's sign (carpopedal spasm with BP cuff inflation 20 mmHg above SBP for 3 min) is a more specific sign of latent tetany/hypocalcemia than Chvostek's sign (facial twitch on tapping facial nerve).

q: What is the standard color coding and outer gauge size of the IV cannula most commonly used for rapid trauma fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion in adults?
e: 18G (Green) and 16G (Grey) large-bore cannulas permit rapid crystalloid and blood transfusion. 20G (Pink) is routine adult IV; 22G (Blue) is small veins/pediatrics; 24G (Yellow) is neonates/infants.

q: Under India's Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016/2018), anatomical human tissue, soiled cotton dressings, and placenta must be segregated into which color-coded bin?
e: Yellow bin/bag is for human/animal anatomical waste, soiled dressings/plaster casts contaminated with blood/body fluids, and expired/discarded medicines for incineration or deep burial.

q: What is the most reliable bedside method to verify initial placement of a newly inserted nasogastric (NG) feeding tube before starting enteral nutrition?
o: Auscultating an air bolus over the epigastrium
Checking an abdominal/chest X-ray confirming tip below the diaphragm in the stomach
Submerging the outer tip in a cup of water for bubbles
e: Radiographic (X-ray) confirmation is the gold standard for initial NG/enteral tube verification; checking aspirate pH (<=5.5) is used for routine ongoing checks. Air auscultation is unreliable and discouraged.

q: Using Naegele's rule, what is the Expected Date of Delivery (EDD) if a pregnant woman's Last Menstrual Period (LMP) started on June 10, 2025?
e: Naegele's rule: LMP + 9 calendar months + 7 days (or subtract 3 months + add 7 days + 1 year). June 10 + 9 months = March 10 + 7 days = March 17, 2026.

q: During the normal postpartum period, lochia progresses in which physiological sequence?
e: Lochia rubra (dark red, days 1–4) -> Lochia serosa (pinkish-brown, days 4–10) -> Lochia alba (yellowish-white, days 10–14+ up to 3–6 weeks).

q: A Rh-negative mother delivers a Rh-positive newborn (Indirect Coombs Test negative). Within how many hours of delivery must Anti-D (RhoGAM) 300 mcg IM be administered?
e: Anti-D immunoglobulin (300 mcg IM) must be administered within 72 hours of birth (and routinely at 28 weeks gestation) to prevent maternal Rh isoimmunization in subsequent pregnancies.

q: What is the normal closing age of the anterior fontanelle (bregma) in a healthy child?
e: The posterior fontanelle closes by 6–8 weeks (1.5–2 months); the diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle normally closes between 12 and 18 months of age.

q: A 6-week-old male infant presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting immediately after feeds, visible peristaltic waves, and a palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Non-bilious projectile vomiting + olive-shaped epigastric/RUQ mass + hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis in a 3–8 week infant are classic for congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

q: What is the total osmolarity of the WHO-recommended low-osmolarity Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)?
e: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS has a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L (Sodium 75, Chloride 65, Glucose 75, Potassium 20, Citrate 10 mmol/L), reducing stool output and vomiting.

q: At a Primary Health Centre (PHC), what is the recommended cold-chain storage temperature inside an Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) for routine UIP vaccines?
e: ILRs at PHCs maintain +2°C to +8°C. Freeze-sensitive vaccines (Pentavalent, DPT, HepB, TT/Td, IPV, PCV) are placed in the upper basket, while heat-sensitive OPV/MR go lower (deep freezers at -15°C to -25°C make ice packs).

q: According to Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), one Sub-Centre (Health & Wellness Centre) covers what standard rural population in plain vs hilly/tribal areas?
e: Rural health tier norms in India: Sub-Centre = 5,000 (3,000 hilly); PHC = 30,000 (20,000 hilly); CHC = 1,20,000 (80,000 hilly).

q: A patient taking Haloperidol develops high fever (40.2°C), severe 'lead-pipe' muscular rigidity, autonomic instability, and markedly elevated serum Creatine Kinase (CK). What life-threatening condition is suspected?
e: NMS is a fatal idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics): fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered sensorium, autonomic instability, and high CK. Immediately stop the antipsychotic and prepare Dantrolene/Bromocriptine.

q: Which medication is the specific reversal agent (antidote) for benzodiazepine overdose such as Diazepam or Midazolam?
e: Flumazenil is a competitive GABA-A benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used for benzodiazepine reversal (use cautiously in chronic users due to seizure risk).

q: Which first-line anti-tubercular drug is notorious for causing peripheral neuropathy preventable by co-administering Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine)?
e: Isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine metabolism causing peripheral neuropathy; Pyridoxine 10–50 mg/day prevents it. Ethambutol causes optic neuritis (red-green color blindness); Rifampicin causes orange-red body secretions.

q: In nursing research, a study design that randomly assigns participants to an intervention group and a control group to establish cause-and-effect is a:
e: True experimental designs (RCTs) include all three hallmarks: Manipulation (intervention), Control group, and Randomization, providing the strongest causal evidence.

q: A patient with right-sided heart failure is MOST likely to exhibit which classic cluster of clinical signs?
o: Pink frothy sputum and pulmonary crackles
Jugular venous distension (JVD), hepatomegaly, ascites, and dependent pitting edema
Isolated S3 gallop with severe orthopnea only
e: Right-sided heart failure causes systemic venous congestion (JVD, hepatojugular reflux, ascites, peripheral edema), whereas left-sided failure causes pulmonary congestion (dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, pink frothy sputum).

q: In a patient with Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH), which combination of lab results is expected?
o: Dilutional hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, and concentrated urine (high urine osmolality)
e: Excess ADH causes free water retention -> dilutional hyponatremia (<135 mEq/L), low plasma osmolality, and inappropriately concentrated urine (high specific gravity). Fluid restriction is first-line management.

q: Which bedside positioning is safest for a patient with acute left-sided pleural effusion undergoing thoracentesis?
o: Sitting upright on the edge of the bed leaning forward over a padded overbed table
e: Sitting upright leaning forward over an overbed table widens the intercostal spaces and allows pleural fluid to pool dependently for safe posterior needle insertion above the upper border of the lower rib.

q: A patient with a T4 spinal cord injury suddenly develops throbbing headache, BP 218/124 mmHg, facial flushing above the lesion, and bradycardia (50 bpm). What is the nurse's FIRST action?
o: Sit the patient upright (high-Fowler's) and check immediately for a kinked Foley catheter or distended bladder
Apply cold packs to the lower extremities
e: Autonomic dysreflexia (in SCI at/above T6) is a hypertensive emergency usually triggered by bladder distension or fecal impaction. First elevate the head of bed to lower BP via orthostasis, loosen tight clothing, and relieve the noxious stimulus.

q: What is the classic clinical triad of Meniere's disease affecting the inner ear?
o: Episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss
e: Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops) manifests with recurrent vertigo, roaring tinnitus, aural fullness, and fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss; managed with low-sodium diet and diuretics.

q: Which anatomical site is recommended as the SAFEST and preferred site for deep intramuscular (IM) injections in adults to avoid sciatic nerve injury?
e: The ventrogluteal site (gluteus medius/minimus located using the palm over greater trochanter and V between index/middle fingers toward ASIS and iliac crest) is free of major nerves and blood vessels.

q: A Stage 3 pressure ulcer (pressure injury) is characterized by:
o: Partial-thickness loss of dermis presenting as a shallow open ulcer or blister
Full-thickness skin loss where subcutaneous fat may be visible, without exposed bone, tendon, or muscle
Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle
e: NPIAP staging: Stage 1 = intact skin non-blanchable erythema; Stage 2 = partial-thickness dermis/blister; Stage 3 = full-thickness into adipose/subcutis; Stage 4 = exposed bone/tendon/muscle.

q: Which chemical disinfectant is standard for high-level cold sterilization of heat-sensitive endoscopes and bronchoscopes?
e: 2% Glutaraldehyde (Cidex) achieves high-level disinfection in 20 minutes and chemical sterilization (sporicidal) after 10 hours of immersion for heat-sensitive scopes.

q: Which fetal heart rate (FHR) deceleration pattern is caused by uteroplacental insufficiency and begins AFTER the peak of a uterine contraction, returning to baseline after the contraction ends?
e: VEAL CHOP: Variable = Cord compression; Early = Head compression (benign); Accelerations = Okay; Late = Placental insufficiency (requires immediate LION: Left lateral, IV fluids, O2, Notify/stop oxytocin).

q: At 20 weeks of gestation, where is the uterine fundus normally palpated during abdominal examination?
o: Midway between symphysis pubis and umbilicus
At the level of the umbilicus
e: Fundal height milestones: 12 wks = symphysis pubis; 16 wks = midway to umbilicus; 20–22 wks = umbilicus; 36 wks = xiphisternum (drops slightly at 38–40 wks with lightening).

q: Which clinical feature reliably differentiates Abruptio Placentae from Placenta Previa in third-trimester antepartum hemorrhage?
o: Painless bright-red bleeding with soft, non-tender uterus
Painful dark-red bleeding with a rigid, board-like tender uterus and fetal distress
e: Abruptio placentae (premature separation of normally implanted placenta) causes severe abdominal pain, dark-red bleeding (or concealed hemorrhage), uterine tenderness/hypertonicity (woody/board-like), and rapid fetal distress.

q: What are the FOUR congenital anatomical defects of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)?
o: ASD, VSD, PDA, Coarctation of aorta
Pulmonary stenosis, VSD, Overriding aorta, Right ventricular hypertrophy
Transposition of great arteries, VSD, LVH, Tricuspid atresia
Aortic stenosis, Mitral regurgitation, ASD, RVH
e: PROV mnemonic for Tetralogy of Fallot: Pulmonary stenosis, Right ventricular hypertrophy, Overriding aorta, Ventricular septal defect. Children adopt knee-chest/squatting posture during 'Tet spells' to increase SVR.

q: A newborn undergoing phototherapy for physiological hyperbilirubinemia requires which essential nursing precaution?
o: Apply oil or lotion liberally to prevent dry skin
Shield both eyes with opaque eye patches and cover the genitalia, turning the infant frequently
Keep the infant fully clothed under the light
e: Eye shields protect the retina from UV/blue-light damage; expose maximum skin surface (diaper only), avoid oils/lotions (burn risk), monitor temperature/hydration, and continue frequent breastfeeding to promote bilirubin excretion.

q: What is the classic 'currant jelly' stool finding accompanied by paroxysmal severe abdominal pain and sausage-shaped abdominal mass in an 8-month-old infant indicative of?
e: Intussusception (telescoping of bowel, typically ileocolic) presents with episodic inconsolable crying drawing knees to chest, sausage-shaped RUQ mass, and blood/mucus 'currant jelly' stools.

q: Rehabilitation of a stroke survivor through physiotherapy to minimize disability belongs to which level of disease prevention?
e: Levels of prevention: Primordial (prevent emergence of risk factors), Primary (health promotion/vaccination before disease), Secondary (early diagnosis & prompt treatment/screening), Tertiary (disability limitation & rehabilitation).

q: In water chlorination, what is the minimum recommended free residual chlorine level in drinking water after a 1-hour contact period under normal conditions?
e: WHO/Indian standard for safe drinking water requires a free residual chlorine of at least 0.5 mg/L after 1 hour contact time (measured by Orthotolidine Arsenite / OTA test).

q: Which defense mechanism is demonstrated when a student who failed an exam blames the examiner for making unfair questions?
e: Rationalization creates logical-sounding excuses for failure, while projection attributes one's own unacceptable thoughts/faults to others (externalizing blame).

q: Before modified Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT), which two drug classes are routinely administered for anesthesia and muscle relaxation?
e: Modified ECT uses a short-acting IV anesthetic (Propofol/Thiopentone/Methohexital) + depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (Succinylcholine) to prevent fractures/injuries while allowing therapeutic cerebral seizure activity.

q: Which lab test is used to monitor the therapeutic effect of oral Warfarin therapy, and what is its specific antidote?
e: Warfarin inhibits Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and is monitored by PT/INR (target usually 2.0–3.0; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical valves); reversed by Vitamin K1 and 4-factor PCC/FFP in severe bleeding.

q: Which part of the human brain regulates vital autonomic functions including respiratory rhythm, heart rate, and vasomotor tone?
e: The medulla oblongata (brainstem) houses the cardiac, vasomotor, and primary respiratory control centers.

q: A patient with myasthenia gravis experiences worsening muscle weakness, ptosis, and respiratory difficulty. Following IV Edrophonium (Tensilon) test, muscle strength dramatically improves within 60 seconds. This confirms:
e: Edrophonium (short-acting anticholinesterase) temporarily improves weakness in Myasthenic crisis (insufficient acetylcholine/anticholinesterase) but worsens weakness in Cholinergic crisis (excess medication; keep Atropine at bedside).

q: In Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), what is the MOST critical life-threatening complication that the nurse must monitor continuously?
o: Ascending paralysis involving the diaphragm causing acute respiratory failure
e: GBS causes acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with symmetric ascending weakness; serial vital capacity / negative inspiratory force monitoring is vital because diaphragmatic involvement causes respiratory arrest.

q: Which hallmark finding on urinalysis and serum chemistry defines Nephrotic Syndrome?
o: Massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema (anasarca), and hyperlipidemia
e: Nephrotic syndrome triad/tetrad: heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/24h), hypoalbuminemia (<3 g/dL), severe edema (periorbital/anasarca), and compensatory hyperlipidemia/lipiduria.

q: For a patient with a mature arteriovenous (AV) fistula in the left forearm for hemodialysis, which nursing action is STRICTLY PROHIBITED on the left arm?
o: Palpating for a thrill every shift
Measuring blood pressure, drawing blood, or inserting IV lines
Keeping the arm clean and dry
e: Never take BP, perform venipuncture, or start IV infusions in an AV fistula extremity, as compression or thrombosis can permanently destroy the dialysis access.

q: Which clinical triad characterizes Cardiac Tamponade (Beck's triad)?
o: Hypotension, jugular venous distension (JVD), and muffled/distant heart sounds
e: Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD) plus pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop in SBP during inspiration) indicates cardiac tamponade requiring urgent pericardiocentesis.

q: In the nursing process, which step involves setting measurable, patient-centered SMART goals and selecting nursing interventions?
e: ADPIE sequence: Assessment (data collection), Diagnosis (problem identification), Planning (SMART outcomes & intervention selection), Implementation (carrying out care), Evaluation (measuring goal attainment).

q: Which position is recommended when administering a cleansing enema to facilitate gravity flow along the natural anatomical curve of the sigmoid colon?
e: Left lateral Sims position places the descending and sigmoid colon below the rectum, allowing enema solution to flow smoothly inward by gravity with minimal cramping.

q: What is the normal adult range for Central Venous Pressure (CVP) measured in cm H2O?
e: Normal CVP is 2–8 mmHg (approx. 3–12 cm H2O). Low CVP indicates hypovolemia; high CVP suggests fluid overload, right heart failure, or cardiac tamponade.

q: How many vessels are normally present in a healthy human umbilical cord?
e: A normal umbilical cord contains 2 umbilical arteries (carrying deoxygenated fetal blood to the placenta) and 1 umbilical vein (carrying oxygenated blood to the fetus) embedded in Wharton's jelly.

q: What is the most common site of implantation in an ectopic pregnancy?
e: Over 95% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, most frequently in the ampullary segment (~70–80%).

q: What is the daily prophylactic dose of Folic Acid recommended during the periconceptional period (1 month before conception through the first trimester) to prevent neural tube defects?
e: 400 mcg (0.4 mg) daily folic acid prevents neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly); women with a prior NTD-affected pregnancy require a higher therapeutic dose of 4–5 mg/day.

q: Which pathognomonic oral lesion appears as small bluish-white spots on an erythematous buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars 1–2 days before the measles rash?
e: Koplik's spots are pathognomonic of Measles (Rubeola). Strawberry tongue occurs in Scarlet fever/Kawasaki disease; Bitot's spots indicate Vitamin A deficiency; Forchheimer spots occur in Rubella.

q: At what age does a healthy infant typically sit without support and develop stranger anxiety?
e: Gross motor & social milestones: social smile 2 mo, head control 3–4 mo, rolls over 5–6 mo, sits unsupported & stranger anxiety 7–8 mo, walks independently ~12–15 mo.

q: Under IMNCI guidelines, what respiratory rate cut-off defines 'fast breathing' (pneumonia sign) in a child aged 2 months to 12 months?
e: IMNCI fast-breathing thresholds: <2 months = >=60/min; 2–12 months = >=50/min; 12 months to 5 years = >=40/min.

q: Which mosquito species is the primary vector for Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika virus transmission in India?
e: Aedes aegypti (tiger mosquito, day-biter breeding in clean stagnant artificial containers) transmits Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika, and Yellow Fever. Anopheles transmits Malaria; Culex transmits JE and Filariasis.

q: The denominator used to calculate the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) is:
e: MMR is expressed as maternal deaths per 100,000 (1 lakh) live births. Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) and Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) are per 1,000 live births.

q: Under India's Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA) 2017, which statement regarding attempted suicide (Section 115) is accurate?
o: It is punished with mandatory imprisonment
A person who attempts suicide is presumed to have severe stress and shall not be tried or punished under IPC Section 309, with a government duty to provide care and rehabilitation
Only courts may authorize emergency psychiatric care
e: MHCA 2017 Section 115 decriminalizes suicide attempts by presuming severe stress and mandating state-provided mental health care and rehabilitation.

q: A patient taking Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) such as Phenelzine must avoid aged cheeses, cured meats, and red wine to prevent hypertensive crisis caused by excess:
e: MAOIs inhibit breakdown of dietary tyramine in the gut/liver, allowing tyramine to trigger massive norepinephrine release and life-threatening hypertensive crisis.

q: Which cells in the gastric mucosa secrete Intrinsic Factor required for Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum?
e: Parietal cells in the stomach fundus/body secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and Intrinsic Factor; autoimmune destruction causes pernicious anemia.

q: In hospital inventory management, ABC analysis classifies medical supplies primarily based on:
o: Annual consumption value / cost (high-value A items vs low-value C items)
e: ABC (Always Better Control) classifies by annual expenditure value (A = ~70% budget, ~10% items); VED (Vital, Essential, Desirable) classifies by clinical criticality.

q: A patient with Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) arrives with severe hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia (Addisonian crisis). What is the immediate priority medication?
o: IV Hydrocortisone (100 mg stat) and IV 0.9% Normal Saline with Dextrose
e: Addisonian crisis is fatal acute glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid deficiency. Immediate IV Hydrocortisone (100 mg bolus) + rapid NS/D5NS fluid resuscitation are life-saving.

q: What is the classic clinical triad of Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor)?
o: Episodic severe headache, profuse diaphoresis (sweating), and palpitations with paroxysmal hypertension
Weight gain, moon face, buffalo hump
e: Pheochromocytoma triggers sudden catecholamine surges causing the classic triad of headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis with severe paroxysmal hypertension. Never palpate the abdomen vigorously!

q: Charcot's triad—fever with chills, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice—is diagnostic of which hepatobiliary emergency?
e: Charcot's triad indicates acute cholangitis (biliary obstruction + infection); adding hypotension and altered mental status forms Reynolds' pentad (septic shock requiring urgent ERCP decompression).

q: Which laboratory value is the best indicator of average glycemic control over the preceding 2–3 months in diabetes mellitus?
e: HbA1c reflects non-enzymatic glycation of hemoglobin over the ~120-day lifespan of RBCs; target for most non-pregnant adults with diabetes is <7.0%.

q: A patient with bacterial meningitis demonstrates involuntary flexion of both hips and knees when the nurse passively flexes the patient's neck. This positive meningeal sign is:
e: Brudzinski's neck sign = passive neck flexion triggers involuntary hip/knee flexion. Kernig's sign = pain/resistance when extending the knee with the hip flexed at 90 degrees.

q: What is the normal adult serum sodium (Na+) concentration range?
e: Normal adult electrolytes: Na+ 135–145 mEq/L, K+ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L, Cl- 98–106 mEq/L, Total Ca2+ 8.5–10.5 mg/dL, Mg2+ 1.7–2.2 mg/dL.

q: When administering an IV infusion of Potassium Chloride (KCl) to treat hypokalemia, which safety rule is ABSOLUTE?
o: Give KCl as a rapid IV bolus over 1 minute
NEVER administer KCl as an undiluted IV push; always dilute and infuse slowly via an infusion pump (typically <=10 mEq/hr peripherally)
Mix KCl only in ice-cold water
Give KCl without verifying urine output
e: Undiluted IV push KCl causes immediate fatal cardiac arrest (asystole). Always dilute, confirm adequate urine output (>=30 mL/hr), and infuse slowly using a rate-controlled pump.

q: In a blood transfusion, what is the MAXIMUM safe duration allowed for infusing a single unit of Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC) from the time it leaves controlled blood bank refrigeration?
e: A unit of PRBCs must be started within 30 minutes of issue and completed within 4 hours to minimize bacterial proliferation; stay with the patient during the first 15 minutes (slow rate) to watch for acute reactions.

q: Which hormone is responsible for the milk-ejection ('let-down') reflex during breastfeeding?
e: Prolactin (anterior pituitary) stimulates milk synthesis/production; Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) contracts myoepithelial cells to cause milk ejection ('let-down').

q: In obstetric terminology, 'Quickening' (first maternal perception of fetal movements) typically occurs at what gestational age in a primigravida vs multigravida?
o: 18–20 weeks in primigravida (16–18 weeks in multigravida)
e: Primigravidae usually feel quickening around 18–20 weeks; multigravidae recognize it earlier around 16–18 weeks.

q: A post-cesarean patient develops unilateral calf pain, warmth, swelling, and tenderness along the deep venous system. Which diagnostic test is the FIRST-LINE non-invasive investigation of choice?
e: Compression Doppler ultrasound is the non-invasive gold standard for diagnosing lower-extremity DVT in pregnancy and the puerperium.

q: Which congenital vitamin/mineral deficiency in children causes bowing of legs, rachitic rosary, widened wrists, and craniotabes?
e: Vitamin D deficiency impairs bone mineralization at growth plates, causing Rickets (craniotabes, frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, Harrison's sulcus, genu varum/valgum).

q: In Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) for stable low-birth-weight (<2,000 g) neonates, how is the baby positioned?
o: Supine in a separate bassinet beside the bed
Upright skin-to-skin between the mother's breasts in a frog-like position with head turned to one side
Swaddled in heavy blankets away from the mother
e: KMC maintains neutral thermal environment, stabilizes cardiorespiratory rhythm, promotes exclusive breastfeeding, and reduces neonatal sepsis and mortality in LBW/preterm infants.

q: Under India's National Vitamin A Prophylaxis Programme, what is the first oral dose of Vitamin A given at 9 months along with the MR-1 vaccine?
e: First dose at 9 months is 1,00,000 IU (1 mL), followed by 2,00,000 IU (2 mL) every 6 months from 16–18 months up to 5 years of age (total 9 doses).

q: What is the Pearl Index used to measure in family planning and reproductive health?
o: Contraceptive failure rate (number of accidental pregnancies per 100 woman-years of exposure)
e: Pearl Index = (Accidental pregnancies × 1200) / Total months of exposure. Lower Pearl Index indicates higher contraceptive effectiveness.

q: Which vaccine is strictly CONTRAINDICATED in pregnant women because it contains live attenuated organisms?
e: Live attenuated vaccines (MMR/MR, Varicella, BCG, Yellow Fever) are contraindicated in pregnancy due to theoretical fetal risk (especially congenital rubella syndrome). Td and inactivated flu vaccines are safe and recommended.

q: Which condition is characterized by persistent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive ritualistic behaviors (compulsions) performed to relieve anxiety?
e: OCD features ego-dystonic intrusive obsessions and neutralizing compulsions; first-line treatments are Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (Exposure & Response Prevention) and SSRIs (e.g., Fluoxetine, Fluvoxamine, Sertraline).

q: What is the antidote for acute organophosphate pesticide poisoning presenting with SLUDGE symptoms (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramping, emesis) and pinpoint pupils?
e: Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic cholinergic crisis (drying bronchial secretions is the primary resuscitation endpoint), while Pralidoxime (2-PAM) reactivates acetylcholinesterase at nicotinic neuromuscular junctions.

q: Which cranial nerve is responsible for visual acuity and visual fields?
e: CN II (Optic) transmits visual impulses from the retina; CN III, IV, and VI control extraocular eye movements (and CN III controls pupillary constriction/eyelid elevation).

q: In nursing ethics, the principle of 'Non-maleficence' obligates the nurse to:
o: First do no harm (avoid causing intentional or avoidable injury)
Respect the patient's right to self-determination
e: Core bioethical principles: Autonomy (self-determination), Beneficence (doing good), Non-maleficence (do no harm), Justice (fairness), Veracity (truthfulness), Fidelity (keeping promises).

q: A trauma patient in the PGIMER emergency ward has BP 78/48 mmHg, HR 136 bpm, absent breath sounds on the left chest, hyperresonance on percussion, and tracheal deviation to the right. What is the IMMEDIATE life-saving intervention?
o: Order a portable chest X-ray first
Immediate needle decompression (thoracostomy) in the 4th–5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary line (or 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line) followed by chest tube
Infuse 2 units of PRBCs before intervention
e: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis—NEVER delay decompression for an X-ray. Immediate needle/finger thoracostomy relieves obstructive shock, followed by definitive intercostal chest drain (ICD).

q: In sepsis resuscitation (Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle), what initial crystalloid bolus is recommended for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or lactate >=4 mmol/L?
o: 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid or 0.9% NS
e: The Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle requires: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, infuse 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension/lactate >=4, and start Norepinephrine if MAP stays <65 mmHg.

q: What is the target Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) for titrating Norepinephrine in an adult ICU patient with septic shock?
e: Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends an initial target MAP >=65 mmHg using Norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor to maintain end-organ perfusion.

q: A postoperative abdominal surgery patient develops sudden wound separation with loops of bowel protruding through the incision (evisceration). What should the nurse do IMMEDIATELY?
o: Gently push the bowel loops back into the abdomen
Cover the exposed viscera with sterile gauze soaked in warm sterile normal saline, place patient supine with knees slightly bent, and notify the surgeon stat
Apply a dry sterile pressure dressing tightly
Give oral water to prevent dehydration
e: Never reinsert eviscerated organs! Keep viscera moist with sterile NS-soaked dressings, flex knees/hips to reduce abdominal wall tension, keep NPO, start IV fluids, and summon the surgical team immediately.

q: Which lung-protective tidal volume setting is recommended for mechanical ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)?
o: 4–8 mL/kg (target 6 mL/kg) predicted body weight with plateau pressure <=30 cm H2O
10 mL/kg actual weight with zero PEEP
e: ARDSNet lung-protective ventilation uses low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg predicted body weight), adequate PEEP to prevent alveolar collapse, and plateau pressures <=30 cm H2O to prevent volutrauma/barotrauma.

q: Which component of the Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) prevention bundle reduces microaspiration of gastric secretions?
o: Keeping the patient completely flat at 0 degrees
Elevating the head of the bed (HOB) to 30–45 degrees, daily sedation vacations, oral care with chlorhexidine, and subglottic suctioning
Routine prophylactic antibiotics for all ventilated patients
e: Evidence-based VAP bundle: HOB elevation 30–45°, daily spontaneous awakening/breathing trials, oral hygiene, DVT/peptic ulcer prophylaxis, and changing circuits only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning.

q: A patient with cirrhosis develops confusion, asterixis (flapping hand tremor), and elevated serum ammonia (140 mcg/dL). How does oral Lactulose improve hepatic encephalopathy?
o: It acidifies colonic contents, trapping ammonia (NH3) as non-absorbable ammonium (NH4+) and promoting excretion via osmotic laxation
It binds bile acids in the gallbladder
e: Lactulose is fermented by colonic bacteria into organic acids, converting absorbable NH3 to non-absorbable NH4+ and expelling it in stool (titrate to 2–3 soft stools/day).

q: A patient with a lower-leg cast complains of excruciating pain unrelieved by IV morphine, paresthesia, and pain on passive toe stretching. What emergency is developing?
e: Pain out of proportion (especially on passive stretch) is the earliest cardinal sign of Acute Compartment Syndrome (5/6 P's). Notify the orthopedic surgeon immediately for cast bivalving/fasciotomy; keep limb at heart level (do NOT elevate above heart or apply ice).

q: Which clinical sign is classic for Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma, an ophthalmic emergency?
o: Painless progressive loss of peripheral vision over years
Sudden severe ocular pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, halos around lights, hazy cornea, and fixed mid-dilated pupil
Itchy watery eyes with seasonal allergies
e: Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes rapid IOP spike (>40 mmHg) with severe eye pain, halos, corneal edema, and rock-hard globe; avoid mydriatics/anticholinergics and treat emergently with pilocarpine, IV acetazolamide/mannitol, and laser iridotomy.

q: In Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), when blood glucose falls to ~200–250 mg/dL while the patient still has ketonemia and anion-gap acidosis, what fluid adjustment is required?
o: Switch IV fluids to a dextrose-containing solution (e.g., D5 0.45% NS) and continue IV insulin at a reduced rate until anion gap closes
e: Ketonemia takes longer to clear than hyperglycemia; adding dextrose at BG ~200–250 mg/dL allows continued insulin infusion to suppress ketogenesis and close the anion gap without causing hypoglycemia.

q: Which dietary teaching is essential for a patient diagnosed with Celiac Disease?
o: Lifelong gluten-free diet avoiding BROW (Barley, Rye, Oats if contaminated, Wheat)
Avoiding all rice and corn products
e: Celiac disease is an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten (wheat, barley, rye). Rice, corn, millet, potatoes, and quinoa are naturally gluten-free and safe.

q: A patient with Parkinson's disease exhibits the classic clinical tetrad (TRAP). What does TRAP stand for?
o: Tremor (pill-rolling resting), Rigidity (cogwheel), Akinesia/Bradykinesia, Postural instability
e: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, causing resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and shuffling/festinating gait.

q: An arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.50, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 23 mEq/L in an anxious patient breathing at 34/min. What is the acid-base imbalance?
e: pH >7.45 (alkalemia) + PaCO2 <35 mmHg (respiratory hypocapnia from hyperventilation) + normal HCO3- (22–26 mEq/L) = uncompensated respiratory alkalosis.

q: Which hallmark sign distinguishes Ulcerative Colitis from Crohn's Disease?
o: Skip lesions anywhere from mouth to anus with transmural fistulas
Continuous mucosal inflammation starting in the rectum and extending proximally with frequent bloody diarrhea
e: Ulcerative colitis causes continuous superficial mucosal/submucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum with bloody stools; Crohn's disease causes patchy 'skip lesions' with transmural inflammation and fistulae anywhere in the GI tract.

q: In a patient with Iron-Deficiency Anemia prescribed oral Ferrous Sulfate, which nurse instruction optimizes absorption?
o: Take with a glass of warm milk and antacids
Take on an empty stomach with Vitamin C (orange juice/lemon water) and expect harmless dark green/black stools
Take immediately with strong tea or coffee
e: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) maintains iron in the absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) state; milk (calcium), antacids, and tannins (tea/coffee) inhibit absorption.

q: After a total laryngectomy, a patient has a permanent tracheostoma. Which crucial safety instruction must the nurse emphasize before discharge?
o: Swimming without protection is safe once healed
Never submerge the neck stoma in water, cover stoma loosely during showering, and carry a medical alert ID stating 'Neck Breather'
Oral mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing works normally
e: After total laryngectomy, the upper airway (nose/mouth) is completely separated from the trachea; rescue ventilation must be given stoma-to-mouth/bag-to-stoma, and water inhalation through the stoma is fatal.

q: Which blood product is specifically indicated for a patient with severe active bleeding and a platelet count of 12,000/mm³?
o: Random Donor or Single Donor Platelets (RDP/SDP)
e: Platelet concentrates are indicated for severe thrombocytopenia (<10,000 prophylactically or <50,000 with active bleeding/procedures). FFP replaces clotting factors; Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen, Factor VIII, and vWF.

q: Which tumor marker is most commonly monitored for follow-up and recurrence of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)?
e: AFP is elevated in Hepatocellular Carcinoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumors. CA-125 = ovarian; PSA = prostate; CEA = colorectal; CA 19-9 = pancreatic.

q: When using the Braden Scale to assess pressure ulcer risk in an ICU patient, what do LOWER scores signify?
o: Higher risk of developing pressure ulcers (<=9 indicates very high risk)
e: Braden Scale evaluates 6 subscales (Sensory perception, Moisture, Activity, Mobility, Nutrition, Friction/Shear) scored 6–23. Lower scores indicate higher risk (<=18 at risk; <=9 very high risk).

q: What is the minimum safe urinary output for a hemodynamically stable adult indicating adequate renal perfusion?
e: Minimum acceptable adult urine output is >=30 mL/hr (>=0.5 mL/kg/hr). Persistent output <30 mL/hr (oliguria) signals hypovolemia, shock, or acute kidney injury.

q: When obtaining a sterile urine specimen for culture and sensitivity from a patient with an indwelling Foley catheter, where should the nurse collect the sample?
o: Directly from the drainage bag spigot
By aspirating with a sterile needle/syringe from the disinfected catheter sampling port after clamping tubing briefly below the port
By disconnecting the catheter from the drainage tubing
e: Always scrub the needleless/rubber sampling port with 70% alcohol and aspirate fresh urine directly via sterile syringe—never collect culture specimens from the drainage bag where bacteria multiply.

q: Which oxygen delivery device delivers the MOST precise, fixed concentration (FiO2 24%–60%) regardless of the patient's breathing pattern, making it ideal for COPD?
e: Venturi masks use color-coded air-entrainment jets to deliver exact FiO2 (24%, 28%, 31%, 35%, 40%, 60%) independent of respiratory rate/depth—the safest high-precision device for COPD.

q: What is the correct formula to convert body temperature from Celsius (°C) to Fahrenheit (°F)?
In blood spill management on hospital ward floors (>10 mL spill), what concentration of freshly prepared Sodium Hypochlorite is recommended by CDC/AIIMS/PGIMER infection control protocols?
o: 1% (10,000 ppm) freshly prepared sodium hypochlorite with 10–20 min contact time
e: Large blood spills (>10 mL) are covered with absorbent material and flooded with 1% (10,000 ppm) sodium hypochlorite for 10–20 minutes while wearing heavy-duty gloves/PPE, then disposed in Yellow/appropriate waste.

q: Which central line care bundle element is MOST effective in preventing Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI)?
o: Maximal sterile barrier precautions, 2% chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, optimal site selection (avoiding femoral), hand hygiene, and daily review for prompt line removal
Changing central lines every 48 hours routinely
e: The 5-point IHI/CDC CLABSI bundle centers on hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers during insertion, 2% CHG-alcohol skin prep, subclavian/IJ preference over femoral, and daily necessity review.

q: Which Korotkoff sound phase corresponds to Systolic Blood Pressure and which corresponds to adult Diastolic Blood Pressure?
o: Phase I = Systolic; Phase V (disappearance of sound) = Diastolic
Phase II = Systolic; Phase III = Diastolic
Phase I = Diastolic; Phase IV = Systolic
Phase III = Systolic; Phase V = Pulse pressure
e: Phase I (first clear tapping sound) records Systolic BP; Phase V (complete disappearance of sound) records adult Diastolic BP.

q: A patient is prescribed an isotonic crystalloid for acute extracellular volume replacement in diarrhea/dehydration. Which IV fluid is isotonic?
o: 0.9% Sodium Chloride (Normal Saline) or Ringer's Lactate
e: 0.9% NS and Ringer's Lactate (RL) are isotonic (~273–308 mOsm/L). 0.45% NS is hypotonic; 3% NS and D10W are hypertonic.

q: When using the Z-track method for intramuscular injection (e.g., Iron Dextran), why does the nurse displace the skin laterally before inserting the needle?
o: To seal the medication deep inside the muscle and prevent painful leakage/staining into subcutaneous tissue
To inject directly into a vein
e: Z-track creates a zigzag needle path once the retracted skin snaps back after withdrawal, locking irritating or staining drugs (like iron dextran) inside the muscle belly.

q: What is the normal baseline Fetal Heart Rate (FHR) range for a term fetus?
e: Normal baseline FHR is 110–160 bpm with moderate variability (6–25 bpm). Sustained <110 bpm is fetal bradycardia; >160 bpm is fetal tachycardia.

q: What defines Primary Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) following a vaginal delivery?
o: Blood loss >= 500 mL within 24 hours of vaginal birth (or >= 1,000 mL after cesarean section / any loss causing hemodynamic instability)
Blood loss occurring 3 weeks after delivery
e: Primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours (>=500 mL vaginal, >=1000 mL CS); Secondary PPH occurs from 24 hours up to 12 weeks postpartum. Remember the 4 T's: Tone (atony #1), Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin.

q: During shoulder dystocia in the delivery room, what is the FIRST-LINE obstetric maneuver performed by the care team?
o: McRoberts maneuver (hyperflexion of maternal thighs onto the abdomen) combined with suprapubic pressure
Pull forcefully on the fetal head
e: McRoberts maneuver + suprapubic pressure (HELPERR) resolves the majority of shoulder dystocia cases by flattening the sacral promontory and dislodging the impacted anterior shoulder. Fundal pressure is STRICTLY contraindicated!

q: Which laboratory triad defines HELLP syndrome, a life-threatening variant of severe preeclampsia?
o: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes (AST/ALT), and Low Platelets (<1,00,000/mm³)
e: HELLP = Hemolysis (schistocytes, high LDH/bilirubin) + Elevated Liver enzymes + Low Platelets; definitive treatment is maternal stabilization (BP control + MgSO4) and prompt delivery.

q: Which probable sign of pregnancy refers to bluish-violet discoloration of the vaginal mucosa and cervix due to increased pelvic vascularity?
e: Chadwick's sign = bluish-purple cervix/vagina; Goodell's sign = softening of cervix; Hegar's sign = softening of lower uterine segment (isthmus).

q: Which copper intrauterine device (IUCD) distributed free under India's National Family Planning Programme provides effective reversible contraception for up to 10 years?
e: Cu-T 380A is effective for 10 years (Cu-T 375 for 5 years) and can also be inserted as emergency contraception within 5 days of unprotected intercourse.

q: At what gestational age is an oral 75 g Glucose Tolerance Test (DIPSI / OGTT) routinely performed in India to screen for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)?
o: At first antenatal visit and repeated at 24–28 weeks gestation
e: National guidelines (DIPSI/MoHFW) screen pregnant women with a single-step 75 g oral glucose test (2-hr plasma glucose >=140 mg/dL diagnoses GDM) at the first ANC booking and again at 24–28 weeks.

q: Which cardinal movement of normal vertex labor occurs immediately AFTER internal rotation as the fetal occiput pivots under the symphysis pubis?
e: 7 Cardinal movements of labor: Engagement -> Descent -> Flexion -> Internal rotation -> Extension (delivery of head) -> Restitution & External rotation -> Expulsion.

q: What is the immediate priority nursing care of a newborn diagnosed with a ruptured or intact lumbar Myelomeningocele prior to surgical repair?
o: Place the infant supine directly on the sac
Position prone (or side-lying), cover the sac with sterile moist warm normal saline gauze, avoid latex, and monitor for hydrocephalus
Apply dry talcum powder to the sac
e: Protecting the neural sac from drying, trauma, and infection (meningitis) is priority #1: prone positioning, sterile moist NS dressing, strict asepsis, latex precautions, and daily head circumference monitoring.

q: Which clinical sign is the classic hallmark of Acute Rheumatic Fever evaluated using the Revised Jones Criteria?
o: Migratory polyarthritis, carditis, Sydenham's chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules (Major criteria)
e: Revised Jones Major Criteria (JONES): Joints (migratory polyarthritis), O (carditis), Nodules (subcutaneous), Erythema marginatum, Sydenham's chorea + evidence of antecedent Group A Streptococcal infection.

q: A 2-year-old child with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) has bilateral pitting pedal edema, moon face, flaky-paint dermatosis, hepatomegaly, and apathy. This presentation represents:
e: Kwashiorkor is edematous protein-energy malnutrition (hypoalbuminemia, bilateral pitting edema, fatty liver, flag sign in hair, apathy). Marasmus presents with severe wasting ('old man's face'), alert/irritable child, and NO edema.

q: Which newborn primitive reflex is elicited by stroking the outer sole of the foot from heel toward the toes, producing dorsiflexion of the big toe and fanning of the other toes?
e: A positive Babinski reflex (upgoing hallux + fanning toes) is NORMAL in infants up to ~12–24 months due to immature corticospinal myelination; in adults it indicates an upper motor neuron lesion.

q: What is the antidote/chelating agent commonly used in acute severe pediatric iron tablet overdose?
e: IV Deferoxamine chelates free circulating iron into ferrioxamine, which is excreted in urine (characteristically turning urine 'vin rosé' pink-orange).

q: What is the standard site for intramuscular (IM) vaccine administration (such as Pentavalent or PCV) in infants under 1 year of age?
o: Anterolateral aspect of the mid-thigh (vastus lateralis)
e: The vastus lateralis (anterolateral mid-thigh) is the largest, best-developed muscle in infants with minimal risk of nerve/vessel injury.

q: Under India's Ayushman Bharat — Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY), what annual secondary and tertiary hospitalization health cover is provided per eligible family?
e: AB-PMJAY provides ₹5 lakh cashless health cover per family per year for secondary and tertiary inpatient care across empanelled public and private hospitals (with senior citizens aged 70+ also covered under expanded AB-PMJAY).

q: Which vaccine indicator printed directly on the vial label changes color irreversibly with cumulative heat exposure to verify vaccine potency in the field?
e: The VVM inner square darkens with cumulative heat; use the vaccine ONLY when the inner square is lighter than the outer circle (Stages 1 & 2). Discard at Stage 3 (matches) or Stage 4 (darker).

q: In epidemiological study designs, what measure of association is calculated from a Case-Control study?
e: Case-Control studies (retrospective, starting with diseased cases and non-diseased controls) estimate strength of association via Odds Ratio (ad/bc). Cohort studies directly calculate Incidence and Relative Risk.

q: In the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), which reporting form is filled by hospital doctors/medical officers for presumptive clinical cases?
e: IDSP weekly surveillance uses 3 forms: Form S (Syndromic — by health workers/ANM), Form P (Presumptive — by doctors/medical officers), and Form L (Laboratory-confirmed — by lab technicians).

q: Which community health worker serves as the key bridge between rural households and the public health system at a norm of roughly 1 per 1,000 population under NHM?
e: ASHA workers (trained female community health activists selected from the village itself, ~1 per 1,000 population) mobilize immunization, institutional delivery (JSY), DOTS, and maternal/newborn home visits (HBNC).

q: What is the incubation period and classic clinical triad of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS)?
o: Sensorineural deafness, congenital cataracts, and congenital heart defects (especially PDA)
Hutchinson's teeth, saddle nose, saber shins
e: Classic CRS triad (Gregg's triad): Sensorineural deafness, Cataracts/glaucoma, and Cardiac defects (PDA/pulmonary artery stenosis). Toxoplasmosis causes hydrocephalus + chorioretinitis + intracranial calcifications.

q: A patient experiencing Alcohol Withdrawal presents 48–72 hours after the last drink with severe agitation, visual/tactile hallucinations, profuse diaphoresis, tachycardia, and disorientation (Delirium Tremens). What is the FIRST-LINE pharmacotherapy?
o: IV/Oral Benzodiazepines (Lorazepam, Diazepam, or Chlordiazepoxide) + IV Thiamine BEFORE dextrose
e: Benzodiazepines (cross-tolerant GABA agonists) are the gold standard for preventing withdrawal seizures and treating Delirium Tremens. Always administer IV Thiamine BEFORE glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy!

q: Which therapeutic communication technique is the nurse using by saying, 'You seem very frustrated about how long your recovery is taking'?
e: Reflection validates and mirrors the patient's underlying emotions, encouraging open exploration and strengthening the nurse-patient therapeutic alliance.

q: A patient started on Risperidone develops sudden painful upward deviation of the eyes (oculogyric crisis) and neck twisting (torticollis). Which emergency medication reverses this acute dystonia rapidly?
e: Acute dystonia (extrapyramidal symptom from sudden nigrostriatal D2 blockade) resolves within minutes of parenteral anticholinergics (Benztropine, Diphenhydramine, or Promethazine).

q: Which cluster of symptoms represents NEGATIVE symptoms of schizophrenia?
o: Affective flattening (blunted affect), alogia (poverty of speech), avolition, and anhedonia
Bizarre disorganized speech and catatonic excitement
e: Negative symptoms ('The 5 A's': Affective flattening, Alogia, Avolition, Anhedonia, Asociality) reflect diminished normal functioning and respond better to atypical (second-generation) antipsychotics.

q: A physician orders Dopamine infusion at 5 mcg/kg/min for a 60 kg patient. The IV bag contains 200 mg Dopamine in 250 mL D5W. What pump rate in mL/hr should the nurse program?
e: Dose needed = 5 × 60 = 300 mcg/min = 18,000 mcg/hr = 18 mg/hr. Concentration = 200 mg / 250 mL = 0.8 mg/mL. Rate = 18 / 0.8 = 22.5 mL/hr.

q: Which broad-spectrum glycopeptide antibiotic requires slow IV infusion (over at least 60 minutes) to prevent histamine-mediated 'Red Man Syndrome' and trough-level monitoring for nephrotoxicity?
e: Rapid IV Vancomycin triggers mast-cell degranulation ('Red Man Syndrome': flushing/pruritus of face/neck/upper torso). Infuse over >=60–90 minutes and monitor renal function/trough levels.

q: Why is Methotrexate administered alongside Folic Acid (or Leucovorin rescue in high-dose regimens)?
o: To reduce folate-depletion mucositis, myelosuppression, and hepatotoxicity while preserving therapeutic efficacy
e: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; folic acid supplementation (or Leucovorin/folinic acid rescue in high-dose oncology) protects healthy dividing cells from severe marrow suppression and mucositis.

q: Which emergency drug is the FIRST-LINE treatment for Anaphylactic Shock, and by what route should it be administered immediately?
o: IM Epinephrine (Adrenaline) 1:1000 (0.3–0.5 mg in adults) into the anterolateral mid-thigh
e: IM Epinephrine (1:1000, 0.3–0.5 mg adult; 0.01 mg/kg child) into the vastus lateralis is the immediate life-saving first-line drug in anaphylaxis, reversing bronchospasm and distributive shock rapidly.

q: Which anatomical structure prevents reflux of gastric contents back into the esophagus, and which structure prevents aspiration into the trachea during swallowing?
e: The lower esophageal sphincter prevents gastroesophageal reflux; the epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet (glottis) during deglutition to protect the trachea from aspiration.

q: Where does the majority of nutrient absorption occur along the human gastrointestinal tract?
e: The small intestine (with plicae circulares, villi, and microvilli) absorbs ~90% of nutrients; iron/calcium primarily in the duodenum, carbohydrates/proteins/fats in the jejunum, and Vitamin B12/bile salts in the terminal ileum.

q: In hospital triage during a mass-casualty disaster using the START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) color-coding system, which tag color is assigned to a critically injured victim with an immediate life threat who has a high chance of survival with rapid intervention?
e: START triage colors: Red = Immediate (life-threatening but salvageable, e.g., tension pneumothorax, uncontrolled hemorrhage); Yellow = Delayed (serious, can wait); Green = Minor ('walking wounded'); Black = Expectant/Deceased.

q: In nursing leadership, which structured handoff communication framework stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation?
e: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is the standardized clinical handoff communication tool endorsed by WHO and Joint Commission to reduce handover errors.
